title: Mid-Ocean Ridges, Trenches and Marine Deposits

cards.h: The sea floor is not flat
cards.b: The ocean floor has mountains longer than any on land, trenches deeper than Everest is tall, and sediments that record Earth's history. These features prove plate tectonics and decide where earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis occur. They are a favourite topic in prelims and in questions on map work.

Continental shelf: gently sloping, up to about 200 m deep, rich in fish and oil. Continental slope: steep drop to the deep sea, cut by submarine canyons. Abyssal plain: flat floor at 3,000 to 6,000 m. Ocean deeps (trenches): narrow, below 6,000 m. The average ocean depth is about 3,700 m.

A mid-ocean ridge is an underwater mountain chain along a divergent plate boundary. Magma rises, cools and forms new crust. The system runs about 65,000 km, the longest mountain chain on Earth.

Examples: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the East Pacific Rise and the Carlsberg Ridge in the Indian Ocean. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge cuts through Iceland, where it rises above sea level.

Harry Hess proposed the idea in 1960-62. Robert Dietz named it. New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides. Vine and Matthews (1963) found magnetic stripes in matching patterns on each side of the ridge. They recorded reversals of Earth's magnetic field. This was strong proof.

Sea-floor rocks are young: none older than about 200 million years, because old crust is destroyed in trenches.

Trenches are deep, narrow troughs at subduction zones, where one plate dives under another. The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific has the deepest point, Challenger Deep, about 10,900 m below sea level. Most trenches lie in the Pacific, around the Ring of Fire.

Other deep trenches: Tonga, Kuril-Kamchatka, Philippine, Java (Sunda), Puerto Rico in the Atlantic.

Seamounts: underwater volcanoes that do not reach the surface. Guyots: flat-topped seamounts. Submarine canyons: cut by turbidity currents (the Hudson canyon). Oceanic plateaus: the Chagos-Laccadive ridge and the Kerguelen Plateau. Volcanic islands: Hawaii, Iceland, Reunion. Iceland sits on both a ridge and a hot spot.

Sediments settle slowly on the sea floor. Terrigenous deposits come from land (mud, sand) and lie near the shore. Pelagic deposits are from the open sea. They include oozes (from shells of tiny organisms: calcareous ooze above the carbonate compensation depth, siliceous ooze below) and red clay (very fine, deepest basins). Volcanic deposits come from eruptions.

Polymetallic nodules hold manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific is the best known. Hydrothermal vents deposit sulphides. Gas hydrates store methane in cold sediments. The International Seabed Authority (Kingston, Jamaica, under UNCLOS 1982) regulates seabed mining beyond national waters.

The Carlsberg Ridge, Central Indian Ridge and Southwest Indian Ridge mark the Indian Ocean spreading system. India holds exploration rights for nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin and sulphides on the Carlsberg and Indian Ridges, granted by the ISA. The Deep Ocean Mission (2021) and the Samudrayaan submersible Matsya 6000 support this.

Likely questions: 'Evidence for sea-floor spreading', 'Why are trenches in the Pacific?', 'Importance of polymetallic nodules'.

  • For evidence: magnetic stripes, young crust, ridge heat flow, drilling ages.
  • Draw a ridge and a trench with arrows showing crust born and crust destroyed.
  • Link nodules to India's critical mineral needs and to the Deep Ocean Mission.
